solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Pest's vacuous ideas blocking subtlety

indicators.note: to block something is to sit in its way, so one piece is lodged inside another

parts.note: a nuance is a fine distinction or subtlety

indicators.note: something vacuous is empty, so only the shell of the word survives with its inside gone

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word, with its middle emptied

explanation.surface: A tiresome person whose empty ideas get in the way of any subtle thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s stands for 'is', linking definition to wordplay. IS goes into NUANCE after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A pest is an annoying person or thing, which is exactly what a nuisance is called in everyday speech.

clue.text: Estate perhaps divided by unknown despot

indicators.note: something divided by a wedge is split open with that wedge sitting in the gap

parts.note: an estate is a type of car, hence 'perhaps'
algebra uses x, y and z for unknown quantities

explanation.surface: A landed estate carved up by some anonymous tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Estate' looks like land, but in Britain an estate is a car with a long rear load space (a station wagon).
explanation.definitionFit: A czar (tsar) was an autocratic Russian emperor, and the word is used generally for any absolute ruler or tyrant.

clue.text: Craving son sent down in casual clothing

indicators.note: in a down entry, sending a letter down moves it lower, so it is lifted out and reinserted further along

parts.note: a T-shirt is an informal garment
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A young man expelled from university, still yearning for something, in his scruffy clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent down' suggests expulsion from university; here the S of T-SHIRT moves down the column, from second place to fifth.
explanation.definitionFit: Thirst is used figuratively for any strong desire or longing, matching craving as a noun.

clue.text: Unbounded lewdness corrupted country

indicators.note: without bounds means without edges, so the outermost letters are removed
corrupted means spoiled or altered, so the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: the word minus its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Unrestrained indecency has corrupted a whole nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupted' reads as the verb of the sentence, but it is the anagram signal working on the trimmed letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweden is a Scandinavian nation, an example of the general class named in the clue.

clue.text: Fearless Pinter forged documents

indicators.note: forged means faked or hammered into a new shape, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: the playwright's name taken as letters
ID is short for identity documents

explanation.surface: The bold playwright Harold Pinter faked some papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forged' looks like the main verb, but it shuffles the playwright's name; 'documents' supplies the last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Intrepid describes someone brave and undaunted, a direct synonym for fearless.

clue.text: Entrance to athletics track at opponent's ground

indicators.note: an entrance is where you go in, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word
a track is a path or way

explanation.surface: The way into a running track at a rival team's stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: The sporting surface hides a simple charade; 'track' is a route, not a running lane.
explanation.definitionFit: In sport, a team playing away is competing at the opposing side's home venue rather than its own.

clue.text: Collection of entertaining posers?

parts.note: surface reading: a group of amusing show-offs who strike poses
setter's reading: a programme made of puzzling questions, set for entertainment

explanation.walkthrough: A poser is also a tricky question, so the 'posers' are not people at all but puzzles put to contestants for viewers' amusement.
explanation.definitionFit: A television or radio programme built around a series of questions is entertainment made from a set of brain-teasers.

clue.text: Nothing in Yorkshire at present time

parts.note: the present moment is now
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Nothing whatever is happening in Yorkshire at the moment.
explanation.walkthrough: Yorkshire is a county in northern England whose dialect is often cited in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Northern English dialect uses this word for zero or not anything, the regional form of 'naught'.

clue.text: Guard regularly arrests confident moneylender

indicators.note: to arrest someone is to seize and hold them, so one piece is held within another
regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of the word
confident means sure

explanation.surface: A security guard routinely detains an overconfident loan shark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guard' and 'arrests' suggest policing; instead every other letter of the guard wraps round SURE.
explanation.definitionFit: A usurer lends money at exorbitant interest, a pejorative term for a lender of cash.

clue.text: Foul water closet finally fixed in work done by you

indicators.note: something fixed in place is lodged inside, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: DIY, do-it-yourself, is home improvement you do yourself

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter of each word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of each of the two words

explanation.surface: A smelly lavatory was finally repaired by somebody doing it themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water closet' tempts you to write WC; instead take the last letter of each word.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something unclean or disgusting, so they are straightforward synonyms as adjectives.

clue.text: Female sightseer visited periodically

indicators.note: calling at intervals means dropping in now and then, so only letters at a fixed spacing are kept

parts.note: the first, fourth and seventh letters, every third one

explanation.surface: A woman tourist who dropped in from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: Take every third letter starting with the first; the spacing is wider than the usual alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun refers to a woman or girl, so it stands for a female person as a noun.

clue.text: Bee perhaps caught in little illustration

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: an inset is a small picture set within a larger one
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A bee captured in a small drawing.
explanation.walkthrough: C for caught comes from cricket scorecards; 'perhaps' tells you a bee is just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A bee is one example of a six-legged invertebrate, hence 'perhaps' marking definition by instance.

clue.text: Choosing building that's changed hands

indicators.note: switching hands means swapping right for left, so one letter is replaced by its opposite

parts.note: an erection is a structure that has been built

explanation.surface: Picking a property that has just been sold to a new owner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changed hands' sounds like a sale; here R (right) in ERECTION becomes L (left).
explanation.definitionFit: An election is a vote by which people choose, so the noun matches the gerund choosing as an act of selection.

clue.text: Section of Bologna police in another Italian city

indicators.note: a section is a part cut from a whole, so the answer is a run of letters lying inside the words

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A unit of the Bologna police force stationed in some other Italian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' is fair because Bologna is itself an Italian city.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoli is the Italian name for Naples, a major city in southern Italy.

clue.text: Advance in stages by putting pressure on bent friends?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to progress by jumps, passing others in turn
second meaning, cryptic: the playground game of vaulting over crouching playmates, pressing on their backs

explanation.surface: Making progress step by step by leaning on corrupt allies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' suggests crooked friends, but they are literally stooping over, and the question mark flags the playful second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to move ahead by jumping past others in turn, and the children's game involves vaulting over bent-down companions.

clue.text: Bond formed by chaps in cycling etc

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other
cycling means going round, so the last letter moves round to the front

parts.note: chaps are men
taken as written

explanation.surface: A friendship forged among the lads on bike rides and the like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' looks like the hobby; it moves the C of ETC to the front, giving CET, which then holds MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Cement is a binding material, and figuratively whatever bonds things firmly together, so it serves as a noun for bond.

clue.text: Pair of cards

parts.note: one card, the ten
the other card, the ace

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: two cards side by side spell the bridge term.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge or whist a tenace is a holding of two high cards of one suit ranked one apart, such as ace and queen.

clue.text: Every so often, lads' round in bar causes pandemonium

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a beam is a long bar of wood or metal

indicators.note: to turn round is to face the other way, so the order is flipped
happening at intervals, so only every other letter is kept

parts.note: the first and third letters

explanation.surface: Now and then the boys buying a round at the pub leads to chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' and 'bar' paint a pub, but the round is a turnaround and the bar is a beam of timber.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedlam, from the old London asylum, means a scene of wild uproar and confusion, a synonym for pandemonium.

clue.text: Hurry about using broken leg — not quite

indicators.note: not quite complete means falling just short, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: bust is informal for broken
the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: Rushing around on a fractured leg, though it isn't quite broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' belongs with 'Hurry' in the definition, not as a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To bustle is to move energetically and busily, rushing around, which is a phrasal synonym for hurrying.

clue.text: Millions in international alliance, one that will never take off

definitions.text: one that will never take off

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: the EU, the European Union
M is the abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: Millions poured into an international body that will never get off the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sounds like a failed project, but it describes a flightless bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The emu is a large flightless Australian bird, so it can never become airborne, a playful cryptic description.

clue.text: Giant bird starts to annoy neighbours

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird

indicators.note: the start of something is its opening, so only each word's first letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: An enormous bird starts to bother the people next door.
explanation.walkthrough: A tit is a small songbird, so the giant bird is a joke the wordplay undoes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titans were gigantic deities of Greek myth, so the word now names any person or thing of enormous size or power.

clue.text: Small branch starts to thrive within investment groups

indicators.note: the start of something is its opening, so only each word's first letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A small branch office begins to flourish inside investment groups.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Within' looks like a container signal, but it is one of the words whose first letter counts.
explanation.definitionFit: A twig is a slender shoot growing off a larger bough of a tree or shrub, a direct description.

clue.text: Conflict prevalent on street

indicators.note: in an across answer, one thing written on another follows it, so the first-named piece goes second

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street
rife means widespread or prevalent

explanation.surface: Fighting is widespread out on the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prevalent on street' reads like a description of where the conflict is, but it is a recipe for building the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Strife means angry disagreement or fighting, a formal synonym for conflict as a noun.

clue.text: Study Thatcher's material for auditors

indicators.note: auditors are, literally, listeners, so the word is to be judged by ear

parts.note: a thatcher roofs with reeds, which sound like this word

explanation.surface: Accountants examining Margaret Thatcher's paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: Thatcher looks like the former prime minister, but it is a roofer who covers houses with dried reeds or straw.
explanation.definitionFit: To read a subject is to study it, especially at a British university, as in reading history.

clue.text: Withdrawn uncouth sort holds beginning of Low Mass

indicators.note: to withdraw is to draw back, so the letters run backwards
to hold something is to grip it inside, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: an oik is British slang for a crude or loutish person

indicators.note: a beginning is the opening, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A shy, boorish fellow takes part in the start of a quiet Low Mass service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low Mass' suggests church; 'Mass' alone is the definition, a physical quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: A kilo, short for kilogram, is the standard unit of mass in the metric system, so it names a measured quantity.

clue.text: Brandy ad enlivened with vocals

indicators.note: to enliven is to stir something up, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A brandy advertisement livened up with a sung jingle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' only joins the two lots of letters that are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: Calvados is an apple brandy distilled in Normandy, a specific example of the spirit.
